description: ChronoCosmos is an interactive astronomical discovery platform that transforms NASA's SPHEREx observations into a visual journey through the changing universe.
summary: ChronoCosmos is an interactive astronomical discovery platform that transforms NASA's SPHEREx observations into a visual journey through the changing universe. By combining infrared astronomy, time-based image visualization, automated motion detection, and citizen science, the project enables anyone to explore the sky across different observation periods and participate in the search for moving and variable celestial objects.
details:
The universe may appear motionless when observed from Earth, but every astronomical object is part of a constantly evolving cosmic environment. Asteroids and comets travel through the Solar System, nearby stars move across the celestial sphere, brown dwarfs exhibit measurable proper motion, and variable stars change their brightness over time. Some objects may even reveal themselves through previously unnoticed movements or unusual infrared signatures.

Detecting these changes traditionally requires comparing astronomical observations collected at different times. This technique has played an important role in astronomy, including the historical discovery of Pluto. However, modern space missions produce enormous quantities of observations that cannot be examined manually by individual researchers.

NASA's SPHEREx mission introduces an extraordinary opportunity to expand this type of astronomical exploration. Launched in March 2025, SPHEREx is conducting repeated surveys of the entire sky in 102 near-infrared spectral channels. These observations provide a unique combination of spatial, temporal, and spectral information that can support investigations of stars, brown dwarfs, asteroids, comets, galaxies, and other astronomical objects.

ChronoCosmos proposes a public-facing web application that makes these observations accessible through an intuitive and engaging interface. Users can enter astronomical coordinates, select a region of the sky, and watch a chronological sequence of SPHEREx images displayed as an animated sky movie.

Instead of manually downloading and processing complex astronomical files, users can immediately explore how a selected region changes between observations.

The platform's central innovation is its Cosmic Time Lens, an interactive visualization environment that allows users to move backward and forward through astronomical observations, compare images, highlight moving objects, and investigate changes in brightness.

Users begin by entering the Right Ascension and declination of a target region. The system retrieves available SPHEREx observations corresponding to those coordinates and organizes them chronologically.

A configurable field-of-view control allows users to select the angular size of the region being investigated. Smaller fields provide a more focused view of individual objects, while larger fields make it easier to follow objects exhibiting substantial apparent motion.

The retrieved observations are aligned using their astronomical coordinate information and displayed as an animated sequence. Users can control playback speed, pause the animation, move frame by frame, and compare selected observation dates.

The platform will also provide a blinking comparison mode inspired by the blink comparators historically used by astronomers. Two images captured at different times alternate rapidly, making positional changes easier to recognize.

A difference imaging mode subtracts suitably aligned and normalized observations to highlight changes between epochs. Positive and negative residuals can reveal potential moving sources, brightness variations, or transient phenomena.

Because infrared observations may differ in calibration, background emission, detector characteristics, and noise, the comparison engine will account for these factors before interpreting apparent changes as astronomical signals.

ChronoCosmos introduces an additional feature called the Motion Signature Engine. This component analyzes chronological images to identify candidate objects whose apparent positions change over time.

The system uses image registration, source detection, positional matching, and motion estimation to identify potentially interesting sources.

For each candidate, the platform can estimate its apparent angular displacement, motion direction, and angular velocity when sufficient observations are available.

Detected candidates are displayed as interactive markers on the astronomical image. Selecting a marker opens a detailed observation panel showing the object's coordinates, observation dates, estimated motion, brightness measurements, and available spectral information.

The system will distinguish between previously cataloged astronomical objects and candidates requiring additional investigation.

Cross-referencing observations with external astronomical catalogs can help identify known stars, brown dwarfs, asteroids, and other sources, reducing unnecessary duplicate discoveries.

ChronoCosmos will also provide a brightness variation analysis tool designed to identify objects that change luminosity between observations.

The platform can construct light curves showing measured brightness as a function of time, with uncertainty estimates and quality indicators.

This capability is particularly relevant for investigating variable stars, although the ability to detect specific variations depends on the observation cadence, spectral coverage, and sensitivity of SPHEREx.

A major feature of ChronoCosmos is its Spectral Explorer, which takes advantage of SPHEREx's 102 infrared spectral channels.

Users can explore selected wavelength ranges, create false-color visualizations, and compare how astronomical objects appear at different infrared wavelengths.

Where the available observations and calibration products permit reliable measurements, the platform can generate spectral energy distributions for selected sources.

The Spectral Explorer can also support combinations of compatible measurements from the six SPHEREx detector arrays to improve visualization sensitivity, provided that the data are appropriately calibrated and combined.

Rather than treating infrared observations as ordinary color photographs, ChronoCosmos will clearly explain that the displayed colors are scientific visualizations representing wavelengths beyond normal human vision.

The platform's Spectral Explorer can help users recognize differences between astronomical objects and identify unusual infrared characteristics that may deserve further scientific investigation.

ChronoCosmos also introduces a citizen science experience called Cosmic Discovery Missions.

These missions are guided astronomical investigations that allow participants to explore selected regions of the sky and search for observable changes.

For example, a participant might receive a mission to investigate a field containing a nearby high-proper-motion star. The application displays observations from different epochs and asks the participant to identify which source has moved.

Another mission might focus on detecting a variable star through changes in brightness.

A more advanced mission could involve identifying a moving candidate that does not immediately match a known astronomical source.

Participants can flag interesting objects, record observations, and submit candidate reports containing coordinates, timestamps, image references, and supporting measurements.

The platform will distinguish between educational discoveries, previously known objects, and genuinely unconfirmed candidates. New object claims will require additional validation and appropriate astronomical follow-up.

To improve the reliability of citizen science contributions, multiple independent participants may examine the same candidate. Their assessments can be combined with automated measurements to prioritize objects for expert review.

ChronoCosmos will not automatically classify every apparent movement as a new astronomical discovery. Image artifacts, noise, contamination, differences in detector response, and processing errors can create false signals.

A dedicated verification process will therefore evaluate candidate quality before presenting objects as scientifically interesting.

The platform will provide optional astronomical overlays from external catalogs and missions, including the European Space Agency's Gaia mission and NASA's WISE and NEOWISE observations.

Gaia data can provide reference positions and proper motions for cataloged stars. Historical WISE observations can offer additional infrared context, particularly for nearby cool objects.

These external observations will be presented as complementary information, with their original epochs, wavelengths, resolutions, and measurement limitations clearly identified.
